Police disperse garment workers attempting to block road in Savar
item.description:
Garment workers in Hemayetpur, Savar, tried to block a road on Wednesday while demanding a minimum monthly wage of Tk30,000, leading to a clash with police. Police fired tear gas shells to disperse the protesters and restore order.
The incident occurred around 8:45am near Bagbari intersection in Hemayetpur.
According to witnesses and police sources, workers initially arrived at their respective factories on time. However, shortly afterwards, workers from several factories stopped working and walked out, gathering on the Hemayetpur-Singair road in an attempt to block it.
The protesters also visited nearby factories that were still operating and urged workers there to stop production and join the demonstration. There were reports that some factories were targeted with bricks and stones thrown from outside, in apparent attempts to vandalise the premises.
The workers eventually gathered at Bagbari intersection and began protesting, disrupting traffic on the road.
Industrial Police and local police arrived after receiving reports of the blockade. When the workers refused to clear the road, police fired tear gas shells to disperse them.
Additional police and law enforcement personnel have been deployed at key locations across the industrial zone, including Bagbari intersection and Hemayetpur. Patrols have also been intensified to prevent further unrest.
Mohammad Mominul Islam Bhuiyan, superintendent of Industrial Police-1, said production had been suspended at 41 factories across the Savar and Ashulia industrial zones amid the ongoing movement for a higher minimum wage.
Of these, authorities at 22 factories have declared indefinite closures under Section 13(1) of the Bangladesh Labour Act, 2006, under the “no work, no pay” provision. Workers at 10 factories have stopped work over wage demands, while nine factories have declared general holidays for Wednesday to prevent untoward incidents amid the unrest.
Law enforcement personnel remain on high alert to maintain order across the industrial areas as workers continue their protests.

item.title: Auto-rickshaw driver killed, 3 injured in bus collision in Jatrabari
item.description:
An auto-rickshaw driver was killed and 3 others, including 2 Qatar-bound passengers, were injured after a bus hit their vehicle in Raerbagh, Jatrabari, Dhaka, on Wednesday morning.
The deceased was identified as Masum Mia, 40. The injured were identified as Md Bashir, 33, and Qatar-bound passengers Kawsar Hossain Rubel, 31, and Al Amin, 30.
The injured were taken to the emergency department of Dhaka Medical College Hospital (DMCH), where doctors declared Masum dead. The 3 injured are receiving treatment.
Bashir's wife said Rubel and Al Amin were scheduled to fly to Qatar at 11:30am on Wednesday. They were travelling by auto-rickshaw from in front of Baganbari Mosque in Raerbagh, Shonir Akhra, towards the main road, where they planned to take a CNG-run auto-rickshaw to the airport.
Her husband was accompanying them, she added.
When the auto-rickshaw reached Raerbagh bus stand, a bus hit it and drove away, causing the vehicle to overturn and injuring all 4 occupants, she said.
Locals rescued the injured, and their families took them to the hospital after being informed of the accident.
Rubel and Al Amin are from Ramganj upazila of Lakshmipur.
Masum was the son of Harun Hawlader of Mondopasha village in Uzirpur upazila of Barishal.
Sub-Inspector Md Selim of the DMCH police outpost confirmed the incident, saying Masum's body had been kept in the hospital morgue and the injured were receiving treatment in the emergency department.

item.title: Police killings, station arson fuel public anxiety
Inmate surge pushes prisons beyond capacity, putting rights at risk
item.description:
Bangladesh’s prisons are grappling with severe overcrowding, with nearly 117,000 inmates being held in facilities designed to accommodate just over 45,000, putting enormous pressure on accommodation, sanitation, healthcare and daily operations.
The scale of the crisis means that, on average, 259 inmates are sharing space intended for every 100. The overcrowding is depriving many prisoners of adequate rest and exposing them to serious health risks.
The situation is particularly alarming for sick inmates, as prison authorities struggle to provide adequate medical care. An increase in arrests in political cases and the prolonged detention of accused persons awaiting trial have further aggravated the problem.
Overcrowding in the country's 68 prisons has thus become more than an administrative challenge, raising serious concerns over human rights and public health.
According to the Department of Prisons, the country's 68 prisons had a combined capacity of 45,186 inmates as of November 22. However, they were holding 116,956 prisoners as of November 23, exceeding their capacity by 71,770.
Of the total inmates, 4,020 are women, while 2,483 are on death row and 170 enjoy division status, according to prison authorities.
Sources said a recent rise in arrests in political cases had added to the pressure on an already overstretched prison system. With a significant number of those arrested being sent to prison, facilities operating beyond capacity are facing further strain.
The impact is being felt across accommodation, food, healthcare, security and overall prison management.
According to prison authorities, the capacity of a prison is determined by the number of inmates it can accommodate while ensuring adequate sanitation, healthcare and security. When the population exceeds twice that capacity, however, every aspect of prison management comes under additional pressure.
A shortage of living space, inadequate ventilation and unhygienic conditions can adversely affect inmates' physical and mental health.
Healthcare is among the most pressing concerns. Although the country's prisons are designed to accommodate just over 45,000 people, more than 116,000 are currently being held there. Providing medical services to such a large population has become increasingly difficult with limited manpower and existing facilities, prison sources said.
Experts warn that overcrowding increases the risk of infectious diseases spreading among inmates. It also makes regular monitoring and treatment difficult for prisoners suffering from chronic conditions such as heart disease, kidney disease, diabetes and hypertension.
Inadequate rest and poor living conditions can further aggravate the health risks for these inmates.
Medical emergencies at night pose an additional challenge. Conditions such as heart attacks, strokes and acute breathing difficulties require immediate medical attention. But overcrowding, limited healthcare facilities and delays in transferring inmates to hospitals can increase the risk of fatal outcomes.
Those concerned say any possible role of delayed treatment or negligence in deaths inside prisons should be thoroughly investigated.
Human rights activists say prison overcrowding cannot be treated simply as a shortage of space. It directly concerns inmates' fundamental rights, human dignity and the state's responsibility to protect them.
Even those detained on criminal charges or convicted of offences retain the right to necessary medical care, safe accommodation and humane living conditions.
Human rights activist Abu Ahmed Faizul Kabir told Dhaka Tribune that overcrowding was undermining inmates' rights to adequate personal space, proper lighting and ventilation, hygienic conditions, rest and medical care.
"Living in cramped conditions increases the risk of infectious diseases and adversely affects inmates' physical and mental health," he said.
"We must remember that imprisonment means restricting a person's freedom, not stripping them of their human dignity and fundamental rights. The prolonged detention of accused persons awaiting trial and delays in the judicial process are making the situation even more complicated," he added.
Faizul Kabir said building new prisons or expanding the capacity of existing facilities alone would not resolve the crisis. Reducing delays in the judicial process, ensuring bail in bailable cases and introducing effective alternatives to unnecessary imprisonment were equally important.
"Alongside expanding prison capacity and improving facilities, it is essential to ensure bail in bailable cases, expedite trials and strengthen alternatives to unnecessary incarceration. The state must take initiatives to transform prisons into centres of reform and rehabilitation, rather than places of punishment alone," he said.
The growing inmate population has also become a major challenge for prison administration. Authorities are struggling to meet the daily needs of a large number of prisoners with limited infrastructure, manpower and medical facilities.
Maintaining discipline while ensuring inmates' security, healthcare and other essential services has placed additional pressure on the administration.
Inspector General of Prisons Brig Gen Md Anwarul Kabir told Dhaka Tribune that overcrowding was a reality the authorities had to manage.
"This is the reality, and we have to accept it. We are trying to manage the situation temporarily with the support and resources available to us," he said.
Asked about inmate deaths and accountability in such cases, he said the authorities immediately investigated the circumstances surrounding each death to determine whether negligence was involved.
"Whenever an inmate dies, we immediately look into the cause of death and whether there was any negligence or anyone was responsible. If anyone is found responsible, departmental action is taken against them," he said.
Those concerned warn that the situation could deteriorate further unless prison infrastructure, healthcare facilities and manpower are expanded in line with the growing inmate population.
They stress that addressing the crisis requires both judicial and administrative measures to reduce the number of prisoners and sustained investment in improving prison accommodation and healthcare services.

item.title: RMG wage talks: Workers cut demand to Tk22,000, owners raise offer to Tk15,700
Child marriage rates return to 2006 levels among adolescent girls
item.description:
Child marriage among adolescent girls in Bangladesh has surged since 2019, wiping out 13 years of progress and pushing the prevalence of marriage among girls aged 15–19 back to levels last recorded in 2006, according to data presented by the United Nations Population Fund (UNFPA).
The Bangladesh Multiple Indicator Cluster Survey (MICS) 2025 shows that 38.9% of girls aged 15–19 are currently married, up from 32.9% in 2019. The increase of 6 percentage points has reversed the progress recorded over the preceding 13 years, when the rate stood at 39% in 2006.
The findings were presented at a dialogue organised by UNFPA in Dhaka on Tuesday, bringing together senior editors and journalists from newspapers, television channels, online news portals and news agencies to discuss proposed reforms to the Child Marriage Restraint Act (CMRA) 2017 and the media's role in addressing child marriage.
Presenting the findings, Iliza Azy, chief of the Adolescents and Youth Unit at UNFPA Bangladesh, highlighted the reversal in progress, drawing on data from MICS, the Bangladesh Bureau of Statistics (BBS) and UNICEF covering 2006–2025.
The data also shows that the proportion of girls aged 15–19 married before 18 increased from 28% in 2019 to 33.9% in 2025. Meanwhile, the proportion married before reaching 15 rose from 7.6% to 9.7% over the same period.
The increase has been widespread, with 51 of the country's 64 districts recording a rise in adolescent marriage rates, 19 of which were statistically significant.
Chandpur recorded the steepest increase in marriages before 18, at 19.8 percentage points, followed by Khulna at 18.9 percentage points.
In 2025, Chapainawabganj had the highest prevalence of girls aged 15–19 married before 18, at 53.5%, followed by Satkhira at 51.3%.
Despite the recent reversal among adolescents, the longer-term figures for women aged 20–24 show some progress. According to MICS 2025, 47.2% of women in this age group were married before 18, down from 64.1% in 2006 and 51.4% in 2019.
However, the survey highlights significant socioeconomic and regional disparities. Child marriage before 18 was recorded among 62.5% of women from the poorest households, compared with 31.5% among those from the wealthiest households.
The prevalence was also higher in rural areas, at 49.4%, than in urban areas, at 42.5%.
A joint UNFPA-UNICEF legal review of the CMRA 2017 and its 2018 Rules identified several gaps that limit legal protection for girls. Although the law criminalises child marriage, it does not automatically invalidate the marriage itself.
The review particularly flagged Section 19, which allows marriage below the legal age under special circumstances with a court order, without specifying a minimum age or providing adequate safeguards. It also identified weaknesses in birth and marriage registration, forged birth certificates, inactive child marriage prevention committees and limited prosecutions.
The joint recommendations include repealing Section 19, setting a uniform minimum marriage age of 18 for both women and men, making child marriages voidable at the request of the child, removing criminal liability for children and extending the complaint-filing period from two to six years.
UNFPA Representative in Bangladesh Catherine Breen Kamkong said a law against child marriage could protect girls only when they were aware of their rights and could access an accountable justice system.
She stressed the importance of accurate media reporting on the law and the lived experiences of girls married as children to help policymakers understand the need for reform and raise public awareness about keeping girls in education.
At the dialogue, media professionals committed to expanding evidence-based and ethical reporting on child marriage and contributing to national efforts to reduce the practice.
The event was organised in partnership with the Embassy of the Kingdom of the Netherlands in Bangladesh, ahead of the inaugural International Day for the Elimination of Child, Early and Forced Marriage on November 27.

item.title: Govt employees face double rent for retaining quarters after transfer
item.description:
Government employees who continue occupying official residences after being transferred outside Dhaka and Chittagong city corporation areas will have to pay double the prescribed rent, the Directorate of Government Accommodation has warned.
In a notice, the directorate asked officials and employees to vacate government quarters within the stipulated period under the Bangladesh Allocation Rules, 1982.
The notice said government employees working in the two city corporation areas are eligible for accommodation allocated by the directorate. However, many fail to inform the directorate after being transferred elsewhere for official reasons, while some continue occupying their quarters beyond the permitted period.
Such practices violate the Bangladesh Allocation Rules, 1982, it said.
Employees authorised to retain government accommodation after being transferred outside the designated areas will be charged double the applicable house rent allowance after the stipulated period, according to the notice.
The directorate said many employees claim they are unaware of the double-rent provision and seek waivers on the grounds that their continued occupancy was authorised. However, it has no authority to waive the additional rent payable to the government under the rules. Similar instructions had been issued previously, it added.
Under Rule 15(2) of the Bangladesh Allocation Rules, 1982, employees allotted government accommodation must vacate it within two months of dismissal, removal from service, expiry of a contractual appointment, resignation, transfer, deputation abroad or retirement.
Rule 15(3) allows the government to extend an employee's occupancy for up to six months in cases of dismissal, removal, resignation, retirement or transfer if retaining the accommodation is essential for their children's education.
Meanwhile, Rule 19(1) stipulates that employees authorised to retain government accommodation must pay rent at twice the rate of their entitled house rent allowance under the national pay scale.
The directorate has urged the concerned authorities to ensure strict compliance with the rules, take necessary action within the stipulated timeframe and inform their subordinate officials and employees accordingly.

item.title: 2 die after inhaling toxic gas in Satkhira septic tank
item.description:
Two people died, and two others fell sick after inhaling toxic gas from a septic tank in Kaliganj upazila of Satkhira district on Tuesday.
The deceased were identified as Mahananda Sarkar, 35, son of Sanatan Sarkar, and Md Arafat, 16, son of Moni Par, of Bareya village.
Local people said Mahananda went to the septic tank of one Ashraf to clean it and died on the spot after inhaling toxic gas.
Later, Arafat also went to see Mahananda’s condition and died there.
Meanwhile, Golam Hossain, joint convener of Tarali union unit of Jatiyatabadi Swechchhasebak Dal and another person also fell sick as they went to the septic tank while trying to rescue those trapped inside.
However, local people rescued Golam Hossain and the other person and took them to Satkhira Medical College Hospital, said Enamul Haque, a member of Tarali Union Parishad.

item.title: Supply of winter vegetables, high egg production drive down egg price
item.description:
Prices of eggs have decreased by Tk20-25 per dozen over a month. In Rangpur, farmers were selling brown eggs at between Tk9.40 and Tk10.25 per egg on 6 November, compared to Tk11 a month earlier. The retail price of the same eggs in Dhaka fell to Tk10.8 per egg, down from Tk13.3 per egg a month earlier. Farmers estimate their production cost per egg at about Tk9.5.
Stakeholders say that the supply of winter vegetables usually triggers a fall in demand for eggs. They say that consumers complain about an egg syndicate when egg prices are high. However, when prices are low, it becomes obvious that there is no syndicate.
Aminur Rahman (48), owner of 7,000 layer hens in three sheds in Hasnabad of Rangpur Sadar, left his father’s tobacco business and started with 2,000 birds four years ago. He is currently producing at 92% (92 eggs per 100 hens each day) but he is concerned about falling egg prices with the arrival of early varieties of winter vegetables. "An increased supply of vegetables has pushed down egg prices, from Tk11.80 per egg earlier to Tk9 per egg. Supply of cheap vegetables reduces demand for eggs. I fear that the price will fall further during the peak season of winter vegetables," he told this author.
A Bachelors student of agriculture science, Rokonuzzaman Mugdho (23), son of Mohammad Mukul of Thakuradaho of Gangachara, has assumed responsibility of running a farm with 9,000 hens. His father began with 1,000 layer birds in 2014. "I am surprised that the price has fallen so early. Chickens lay more eggs during the winter, and availability of vegetables normally causes the egg price to fall. The market rate of our eggs has declined by almost Tk2 per piece, and the peak season of vegetables is yet to arrive," he said. His father added: "I don't worry too much about the market, I focus on my own farming and business. Layer is a long-term investment and in the short term it can be frustrating. No one can control the price, other than the market itself."
Khandakar Abu Sayeed, a school teacher and poultry farmer in Poran area of Pirgachha, started layer farming with 1,000 birds in 2011. Some 17,000 of his 20,000 hens are laying eggs now. He mentioned that lower production of vegetables and fish pushes up the demand for eggs during the summer when egg supply is usually low. "In winter, vegetables are abundant, commercial egg production increases by at least 5 per cent, and production of duck eggs by 20% or so," he said, explaining the fall in egg prices.
Abdus Salam (35), a trader at Taraganj Bazar, Rangpur, used to sell 7 or 8 thousand eggs at Tk11 each day only a month ago. Despite the price fall by Tk1.5 per egg in his area, he can’t sell more than 5,000 eggs each day now. "Earnings of working people and low income people have fallen, and during winter they buy vegetables, that's why demand for eggs fell," he argued.
In the business hub of Saidpur in northern district of Nilphamari, Shafiqul Islam (54), owner of a wholesale store, said that the price of eggs fluctuates with demand and supply. "Higher supply of eggs and availability of vegetables prompted a price decline." He added that "some people blame producers and traders for price volatility, without truly understanding the market."
Kazi Zahin Hasan, director at Kazi Farms, observed that vegetables and eggs are substitutes for each other. "When winter vegetables become available, consumers prefer to buy winter vegetables, and buy fewer eggs. So the demand for eggs falls in winter, and the price of eggs also falls," he said. “Earlier this year, in summer, we saw that excessive rain flooded vegetable fields, and reduced the supply of vegetables. That prompted consumers to buy more eggs. The demand for eggs increased, and the price also increased. Many government officers expect the price of eggs to be stable, but this expectation is not realistic. When supply exceeds demand, the price will be low. When demand exceeds supply, the price will be high."

item.title: Nine more children die with measles symptoms
item.description:
Nine more children died with measles symptoms in the 24 hours until 8am on Tuesday, while 1,351 suspected and confirmed cases were reported across the country, the Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS) said.
With the latest fatalities, the number of deaths from suspected measles has risen to 1,256 since March 15. No deaths from confirmed measles were reported during the latest 24-hour period, keeping the confirmed death toll at 105.
The combined death toll from confirmed measles and measles-like symptoms has now reached 1,361 since March 15.
The DGHS said 1,283 suspected cases and 68 confirmed cases were reported in the 24 hours until 8am Tuesday.
Since March 15, the country has recorded 259,190 suspected cases and 26,300 confirmed cases, according to the latest DGHS data.
A total of 231,999 patients with suspected measles have been admitted to hospitals nationwide since March 15. Of them, 223,158 have been discharged, the release added.

item.title: Govt plans 3,000 electric buses to overhaul Dhaka’s public transport
item.description:
The government plans to introduce 3,000 modern, environment-friendly electric buses in phases to bring discipline to Dhaka’s chaotic public transport system, improve passenger services and reduce air pollution.
The initiative will initially be launched under government management through the Bangladesh Road Transport Corporation (BRTC), with plans to gradually bring private bus operators under the new system.
The plan was announced at a meeting on public transport reform and implementation of the "gross-cost" model under the World Bank-funded Bangladesh Clean Air Project (BCAP) at the Road Transport and Bridges Ministry on Tuesday.
Road Transport, Railways and Shipping Minister Shaikh Rabiul Alam chaired the meeting.
The minister said the government aims to make Dhaka’s public transport system modern, safe, affordable and passenger-friendly through the phased introduction of 3,000 electric buses.
He said merely increasing the number of buses would not resolve the problems, stressing the need for structural changes to the existing operational system.
The transformation could take two to three years, with World Bank support.
Under the proposed gross-cost model, buses will operate through tripartite agreements involving the Dhaka Transport Coordination Authority (DTCA), bus operators and vehicle suppliers, replacing the conventional route-permit-based system.
Fares collected from passengers will be deposited with the authorities, which will pay operators at a fixed rate per kilometre based on compliance with prescribed service standards, rather than passenger numbers or fare collections.
The model is expected to reduce unhealthy competition among buses for passengers, ensure adherence to schedules and improve transparency and accountability in operations.
The introduction of electric buses is also expected to reduce vehicle emissions and improve air quality.
However, the initiative will require charging infrastructure, maintenance facilities, skilled manpower, route restructuring and effective monitoring.
State Minister for Road Transport and Railways Habibur Rashid, Road Transport and Highways Division Secretary Dr Mohammed Ziaul Haque, World Bank Division Director for Bangladesh and Bhutan Jean Pesme, representatives of the World Bank and senior officials concerned attended the meeting.

item.title: SRB: No cause for public alarm over December rumours
item.description:
There is no reason for the public to be alarmed about November, December or January despite various claims circulating on social media about December, said Lieutenant Colonel Md Hafizur Rahman, commanding officer of Special Response Battalion (SRB)-4.
He made the remarks in response to questions from journalists at a press conference at the SRB Media Centre in the capital's Karwan Bazar on Tuesday.
He said people had encountered similar warnings in the past and urged the public not to be anxious.
The SRB official said workers' recent demands for higher wages were legitimate, but some saboteurs had used the protests as a cover to carry out acts of vandalism.
He added that various statements and warnings about December had been circulating on social media.
According to Hafizur, a significant number of people allegedly involved in sabotage, including crude bomb explosions and vehicle arson, had been arrested.
He thanked members of the public for helping prevent such incidents, saying many suspected saboteurs had been apprehended by local residents and handed over to police.
“We are doing our utmost. I would like to extend a special thanks to the local residents, as many of these saboteurs were apprehended by the courageous public and handed over to the police,” he said.

item.title: 174 undocumented Bangladeshis return from Libya
item.description:
A total of 174 undocumented Bangladeshis who were stranded in Libya and wished to return home voluntarily have been repatriated.
They arrived in Dhaka at 4:45am on Tuesday aboard Buraq Air flight UZ-222.
According to the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, the repatriation was carried out with the joint cooperation of the Bangladesh Embassy in Libya, the Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment, the Libyan government and the International Organization for Migration (IOM).
Most of the returnees had entered Libya illegally after being lured and assisted by human traffickers, hoping to reach Europe by sea, the ministry said. Many reportedly faced abduction and torture in Libya.
Officials from the foreign ministry, other relevant ministries and IOM welcomed them at Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport in Dhaka.
The foreign ministry urged the returnees to share their harrowing experiences to raise public awareness about the risks of irregular migration.
IOM provided each returnee with travel expenses, food supplies and basic medical care, as well as temporary accommodation where necessary.
The ministry also said it was working with the Bangladesh Embassy in Libya, the Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment and IOM to safely repatriate other Bangladeshis held at detention centres across Libya.

Ex-MP Azizul Islam sent to jail in Explosive Substances Act case
item.description:
A Dhaka court on Tuesday sent former Jessore-6 independent MP Mohammad Azizul Islam to jail after rejecting his bail petition in an Explosive Substances Act case filed with Mohammadpur Police Station.
Dhaka Metropolitan Magistrate Hasibuzzaman passed the order on Tuesday following an application by the investigation officer, Sub-Inspector Md Khair Uddin Bhuiyan of the Detective Branch's (DB) Tejgaon zone.
SI Md Mizanur Rahman of the prosecution department confirmed the matter.
Azizul Islam's lawyer, Md Kayes Ahmed Arnab, sought bail on his behalf.
The hearing was held in the judge's chamber without producing the accused before the court. After hearing both sides, the court rejected the bail petition and ordered that he be sent to jail.
According to the investigation officer's application, several accused named in the case, along with unidentified individuals, gathered near Beribadh Tin Rasta in Mohammadpur around 7:55pm on November 18 with plans to carry out subversive activities.
Acting on a tip-off, a DB team from the Tejgaon division raided the area around 8:50pm. Several named suspects were detained, while the others fled.
During the operation, police seized around 140 grams of a yellow, sulphur-like substance wrapped in a blue polythene packet from one of the detained suspects. Preliminary interrogation suggested that the substance had been kept for making crude bombs, the application said.
Police later filed a case under the Explosive Substances Act with Mohammadpur Police Station over the incident.
Based on information obtained during the investigation, a DB team from the Tejgaon zone arrested Azizul Islam from Lalmatia in Mohammadpur around 4:20pm on November 23.
Azizul Islam is the son of the late Khandaker Rafiquzzaman of Brahmakati area under Keshabpur Municipality in Jessore. He had been living in a residence in Block A/P of Lalmatia.
He is also a former joint convener of the Keshabpur upazila unit of Bangladesh Chhatra League.

item.title: Shafiqur leaves Australia for home, cancels Malaysia trip
item.description:
Leader of the Opposition and Bangladesh Jamaat-e-Islami Ameer Dr Shafiqur Rahman left Sydney for home on Tuesday after completing a four-day visit to Australia, cancelling his planned one-day trip to Malaysia due to an urgent necessity.
In a post on his verified Facebook post, Shafiqur Rahman said he had been deeply moved by the warmth and hospitality shown by expatriate Bangladeshis during his visit.
He said expatriate Bangladeshis cherished the country, dreamed of its future and wanted to contribute to its development, adding that Bangladesh had a responsibility to give them and all Bangladeshis living abroad the respect they deserved.
The opposition leader said he suspended the planned one-day trip to Malaysia due to an urgent necessity, expressing hope of meeting expatriate Bangladeshis there in the near future.
During the Australia visit, he attended several receptions, discussion sessions and community gatherings involving expatriate Bangladeshis, professionals, academics and community representatives in Sydney and Canberra. Leading a delegation, Shafiqur left Dhaka for Australia on November 20.

item.title: Experts discuss feasibility of solar-powered advanced cold storage technology
item.description:
Environment, Forest and Climate Change Minister Abdul Awal Mintoo emphasized the expansion of modern solar-powered cold storage technology to reduce post-harvest losses, preserve the quality of fruits and vegetables, and improve farmers’ incomes. He said that linking cold storage facilities with temperature-controlled transportation would enable farmers to bring a greater share of their produce to market, reducing waste and creating new income opportunities.
The Minister made the remarks as chief guest at the closing event of the international research project titled “Feasibility Research of Solar Electric-Based Cold Storage Equipped with Low-temperature Latent Heat Material for Fruits and Vegetables in Bangladesh Climate Conditions,” held on Tuesday, 24 November, at Hotel InterContinental in Dhaka.
He noted that agriculture plays a vital role in Bangladesh’s economy, food security, and rural livelihoods. However, climate change, high temperatures, insufficient cold storage facilities, and irregular electricity supply contribute to substantial post-harvest losses. Addressing these challenges requires the expansion of modern technologies and renewable-energy-based storage solutions.
Referring to a pilot solar-powered cold storage facility installed at an agricultural farm in Rajshahi, the Minister said the technology had been developed with Bangladesh’s climate, agricultural practices, and electricity supply conditions in mind. Lessons from the project could help establish more reliable and environmentally sustainable cold storage facilities in other agricultural regions.
He added that the research findings and pilot experience could inform an integrated cold chain system combining pre-cooling, cold storage, temperature-controlled transportation, and digital temperature monitoring. Such an approach could preserve product quality, strengthen local technical capacity, and support low-carbon agricultural infrastructure.
The international research project was implemented under the leadership of the Korea Institute of Industrial Technology (KITECH), South Korea, in cooperation with Bangladesh’s Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change. Financial support was provided by the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP) and the Climate Technology Centre and Network (CTCN). Pacific Solar & Renewable Energy Ltd., Bangladesh, participated as the local industry partner.
The project aimed to evaluate the technical and financial feasibility of a sustainable, energy-efficient, and environmentally friendly cold storage system suited to Bangladesh’s climatic conditions.
The project integrates solar panels with Thermal Energy Storage (TES) and Latent Heat Material (LHM) technology. By storing cooling energy, the system can help maintain stable temperatures inside cold storage chambers when sunlight is unavailable or solar power generation decreases. This creates the potential for an alternative preservation solution in areas with limited electricity supply.
The pilot cold storage system in Rajshahi includes separate pre-cooling and cold storage chambers, solar power generation, thermal energy storage, and temperature-control technology. The project evaluated operational performance, suitability for local weather, technical and financial feasibility, and prospects for scaling up. Technical training for local operation and maintenance was also undertaken.
Speakers at the closing event included Dr. Nurun Nahar, Additional Secretary of the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change; Dr. Kim Jong Yeol, Principal Researcher and Project Leader at KITECH; Youngjin Shin, Director of EST Co., Ltd., South Korea; and expert Dr. Inhan Kim. Dr. Mustafa Hasan, Research Director-in-Charge of the Business Research & Consultancy Centre (BRCC), American International University-Bangladesh (AIUB), also attended.
The Minister thanked UNEP, CTCN, KITECH, local industry partners, researchers, experts, and farmers involved in the initiative. He encouraged further innovative, environmentally sustainable, and technology-driven projects in Bangladesh and expressed hope for continued technical cooperation with South Korea and international development partners to expand modern cold storage technology to other agricultural regions.
Representatives of the ministry, Department of Environment, research institutions, local project partners, NGOs, the agriculture and transport sectors, and print and electronic media attended the event.
This Bangladesh–South Korea technology collaboration represents an important step toward renewable energy integration, climate-resilient technologies, and modern cold chain infrastructure in agriculture. Lessons from the project could contribute to reduced post-harvest losses, stronger food security, and more sustainable agricultural infrastructure.

item.title: Canada vows faster visas, more jobs for skilled Bangladeshis
item.description:
Canada has pledged to expedite and simplify visa processing for Bangladeshi travellers, students and businesspeople, while expressing interest in recruiting skilled workers from Bangladesh and expanding cooperation in cybersecurity.
The assurances came from Weldon Epp, assistant deputy minister for the Indo-Pacific at Global Affairs Canada, during a courtesy call on Home Minister Salahuddin Ahmed at the Secretariat on Tuesday.
Foysal Hasan, deputy chief information officer of the Home Ministry, said the meeting discussed issues of mutual interest, including curbing irregular migration, exporting skilled manpower, cybersecurity, joint investment and resolving the Rohingya crisis.
At the outset, the home minister described Bangladesh and Canada as longstanding friends and development partners.
In response, Epp said that despite efforts to balance its immigration policy, Canada remained interested in welcoming talented Bangladeshi students and skilled professionals.
He assured the minister that visa processing for legitimate travellers, students and businesspeople from Bangladesh would be made faster and easier.
Salahuddin Ahmed urged Canada to recruit skilled workers from Bangladesh through legal channels in line with its labour market needs.
He said Bangladesh had a large pool of trained professionals in nursing, medical technology, home care, marine services and hospitality. Canada could help develop the required workforce by sending trainers to Bangladesh or establishing specialised training academies through joint initiatives.
Welcoming the proposal, Epp said Canada's economy had a growing demand for skilled workers, particularly nurses and caregivers.
The two sides also discussed expanding bilateral trade and investment. The home minister expressed Bangladesh's interest in acquiring advanced technology, including river and coastal patrol vessels for the Coast Guard and cybersecurity and communication equipment for the police.
On the Rohingya crisis, Epp said Canada had increased the number of Rohingya refugees it resettled from Bangladesh despite its efforts to limit overall immigration.
He said Canada was also working to encourage greater involvement by regional countries, particularly members of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN), in resolving the crisis.
Highlighting Bangladesh's generosity in sheltering a large Rohingya population, Salahuddin said China, ASEAN and the international community should increase pressure on Myanmar following the International Court of Justice (ICJ) ruling.
He stressed the need to ensure citizenship, access to safe land and livelihood opportunities so that the Rohingya could return to their homeland voluntarily.
The minister also described cyber fraud, drug trafficking and human trafficking originating from Myanmar as serious regional and global security threats, calling for coordinated efforts to combat the crimes.
Canadian High Commissioner to Bangladesh Ajit Singh, Home Ministry Additional Secretary (Political and Immigration) Dr Ziauddin Ahmed, Joint Secretary of the Political-1 Wing Rebecca Khan, Canadian High Commission Political Counsellor Marcus Davis, Head of Aid Suzanne Quinn, Trade Commissioner Kamal Uddin and senior officials from both sides attended the meeting.

item.title: Shama: Hasina’s return announcement ‘political stunt’
item.description:
State Minister for Foreign Affairs Shama Obaed Islam has said diplomatic efforts are under way to bring back convicted fugitives and those accused of ordering killings during the July-August uprising under extradition arrangements.
She made the remarks while responding to questions from reporters at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs on Tuesday.
Dismissing reports that Sheikh Hasina might return to Bangladesh on December 16 or 17 as “political stunt”, Shama said the former prime minister would be arrested and sent to jail if she returned, and that the law would take its own course.
She said no one knew the whereabouts or plans of the former prime minister since she fled the country, adding that these were not relevant to the government's efforts to secure the return of those accused of crimes.
The state minister said Bangladesh maintained regular diplomatic communication with the Indian government to bring back those involved in killings, enforced disappearances and bloodshed during the July-August period, including the alleged killers of Sharif Osman Hadi and those accused of ordering the violence.
Regarding speculation about Hasina's possible return in December, Shama said such publicity was nothing more than an attempt to put ordinary Awami League leaders and activists at risk. She said it was pointless for Hasina, having left her party's leaders and activists behind, to attempt to create instability or unrest in Bangladesh.
She added that the positions of the foreign and law ministries on the matter were clear.
Asked whether Hasina could renew or apply for a passport or national identity card (NID), Shama referred to constitutional provisions, saying the government was not obliged to issue passports, NIDs or other documents to anyone convicted and sentenced for crimes against humanity. She said the government would not deviate from those provisions.
On the legal jurisdiction of Bangladesh's diplomatic missions abroad, the state minister said the country's 84 missions were considered part of its territory. She added that if the person concerned visited any of those missions abroad, she would be arrested there.

item.title: Chief prosecutor: Hasina’s request for aircraft to return to Bangladesh nothing but madness
item.description:
Chief Prosecutor Md Aminul Islam has described ousted former prime minister Sheikh Hasina’s request for an aircraft to bring her back to Bangladesh as “nothing but madness”.
“Sending an aircraft to bring a death-row convict back to the country would be unprecedented. Sheikh Hasina’s request for an aircraft is nothing but madness,” he said.
He made the comments while responding to questions from journalists at his office at the International Crimes Tribunal on Tuesday.
On the prosecution's position in the case against Ziaul Ahsan, Aminul Islam said: “Criminals against humanity like Ziaul Ahsan are rare in world history. The prosecution seeks the death penalty for him, along with the confiscation of all his property.”
Regarding the progress of the trial of the Awami League as a political party, the chief prosecutor said the investigation into the party's alleged role as a terrorist organisation was ongoing.
He added that the activities of its fugitive leaders were making the party's members' alleged involvement in terrorism and killings increasingly clear.
Hasina, who has been living in exile in India for more than two years, wants to return to Bangladesh on December 16, Victory Day, reports Reuters.
Her spokesperson told the British news agency on Tuesday that she had asked the government to arrange an aircraft operated by state-owned Biman Bangladesh Airlines to bring her home.

item.title: Six members of ‘Four-Star Group’ arrested in Mirpur
item.description:
Six members of the alleged "Four-Star Group" criminal gang have been arrested in Mirpur with firearms, ammunition, locally made weapons and narcotics.
The arrests were made during a special operation conducted by Special Response Battalion (SRB)-4 on Monday night, the force said in a statement on Tuesday morning.
SRB-4 said foreign-made pistols, ammunition, a large quantity of locally made weapons and narcotics were recovered during the operation.
The force said further details would be disclosed later.

item.title: 10 injured in clash during Awami League procession in Gopalganj
item.description:
Ten people were injured in a clash between two groups during an Awami League procession in Kotalipara upazila of Gopalganj on Monday evening. Five shops were also vandalized during the incident in South Hiron village.
The procession was organised despite the ban on the Awami League's activities.
Three of the injured — Mikail Islam, 52, Mashiur Rahman, 42, and Zayed Sheikh, 36 — were admitted to Kotalipara Upazila Health Complex. As Mikail's condition deteriorated, he was transferred to Gopalganj Medical College Hospital for advanced treatment.
According to local sources, members and activists of the Awami League, Jubo League and the banned Bangladesh Chhatra League took part in the procession on Monday evening.
When the procession reached South Hiron village, an argument broke out between Mashiur Rahman, a Jubo League leader and prospective chairman candidate in the upcoming Hiron Union Parishad election, and Shafiqul Islam, brother of another prospective candidate, Munshi Raich Uddin.
The argument escalated into a clash, leaving 10 people injured and five shops vandalized.
Mashiur Rahman said the group had gone to South Hiron village as part of the procession when Shafiqul Islam and his associates attacked them, injuring several people, including himself.
Mashiur also alleged that Shafiqul's brother, Munshi Raisuddin, was involved with Jamaat-e-Islami.
Denying the allegation, Shafiqul said his elder brother lived abroad and was not involved in politics. He acknowledged his own longstanding association with the Chhatra League and alleged that he was attacked first because of rivalry over the upcoming Union Parishad election.
Shafiqul claimed that several people from his side, including himself, were injured and that five of their shops were vandalized and looted.
Kotalipara police station Officer-in-Charge Nayan Chandra Debnath said he was aware of the clash but had received no written complaint from either side.
He said police would investigate the incident and take appropriate legal action if a complaint was filed.

item.title: PM reaches Swarnadwip to witness joint military exercise
item.description:
Prime Minister Tarique Rahman reached Swarnadwip in Noakhali on Tuesday to witness a special joint training exercise involving the Army, Navy and Air Force.
The helicopter carrying the prime minister landed on the island at 11:30am, around an hour after he left Dhaka, said PM’s Deputy Press Secretary Jahidul Islam Rony.
Tarique is scheduled to witness the final exercise of "Joint Special Forces Exercise-1-2026", organised for the first time with the participation of special forces from all three services of the Bangladesh Armed Forces.
During the visit, the prime minister will also view a display of military equipment developed using domestic technology and observe various activities of officers and personnel of the three services at the exercise ground.
The Army's Para Commando Brigade, the Navy's SWADS and the Air Force's 501 Air Regiment are taking part in the exercise.
Tarique is scheduled to return to Dhaka by helicopter in the afternoon.

item.title: 101 BGB platoons deployed in 8 districts
item.description:
A total of 101 platoons of Border Guard Bangladesh (BGB), including two battalions in Gopalganj, have been deployed in eight districts to maintain law and order, ensure public security and deal with any untoward situation.
The other districts are Dhaka, Gazipur, Narayanganj, Mymensingh, Faridpur, Chittagong and Cox's Bazar.
Acting on the directives of the Ministry of Home Affairs, the deployed BGB personnel are performing their duties in coordination with the respective district administrations and other law enforcement agencies, said BGB headquarters public relations officer Shariful Islam on Tuesday morning.
They are strengthening security and surveillance at key installations, industrial zones and other important locations to prevent disorder, violence and activities that could pose a threat to public safety.
Meanwhile, the BGB headquarters is maintaining technology-based surveillance through its monitoring cell to closely observe the situation on the ground and ensure coordination.
Live footage collected through drones, body-worn cameras and other modern technologies is being monitored round the clock.
The BGB said its members were performing their assigned duties in maintaining internal law and order alongside their regular responsibilities at the border, with the highest degree of professionalism, discipline and patience.
The force remains committed to ensuring the safety of people's lives and property, keeping normal movement and daily activities uninterrupted, and taking necessary precautionary measures to deal with any untoward situation.

item.title: Owners offer Tk15,800, workers demand Tk22,000 in wage talks
item.description:
The Minimum Wage Board will resume discussions on garment workers' minimum wages at 2pm on Tuesday after failing to reach an agreement between factory owners and workers' representatives over their revised proposals.
The owners have proposed a minimum monthly wage of Tk15,800, while the workers' side has lowered its demand to Tk22,000, leaving a gap of Tk6,200.
At Monday's meeting, held at the board's office in Segunbagicha, Dhaka, both sides revised their earlier proposals. The owners raised their initial offer of Tk15,000 to Tk15,800, while the workers lowered their demand from Tk32,000 to Tk22,000.
Sources familiar with the board said neither side accepted the other's revised proposal.
After the meeting, workers' representative Babul Akhter said the owners' proposal was neither acceptable nor reasonable. He said the workers' side might revise its proposal further after consulting senior labour leaders and expected the owners to come up with a new offer.
Minimum Wage Board Chairman Syed Azad Subhani said discussions were ongoing and information gathered from visits to small, medium and large factories across the country had also been presented.
He said the board was considering inflation, the number of family members dependent on workers, employers' financial capacity, the condition of small and medium-sized factories, and Bangladesh's competitiveness in the international market.
The government formed a six-member Minimum Wage Board on November 1 following protests by garment workers demanding higher wages.
At the board's second meeting on November 9, the workers' side proposed a minimum monthly wage of Tk32,000. The owners' proposal was scheduled to be submitted on November 16, but that meeting was postponed.
Monday's meeting was chaired by board chairman Syed Azad Subhani, with representatives of workers, factory owners and other members present. BGMEA President Mahmud Hasan Khan and Bangladesh Mukto Garment Sramik Union Federation General Secretary Rashedul Alam attended as experts.
Labour unrest continued in industrial areas on Monday despite the ongoing negotiations.
In Gargaria Masterbari area of Sreepur, Gazipur, workers blocked the Dhaka-Mymensingh highway demanding higher wages. Law enforcement personnel dispersed them using sound grenades and tear gas, disrupting traffic.
Production was suspended at around 55 factories in Gazipur amid the unrest.
In Ashulia, authorities declared a holiday at 33 factories on Monday, while another 22 were already closed under Section 13(1) of the Bangladesh Labour Act, 2006.
Tuesday's meeting is expected to focus on narrowing the gap between the two proposals and reaching an acceptable wage structure.

item.title: Tazreen fire victims still await rehabilitation 14 years on
item.description:
The Tazreen fire remains one of the deadliest industrial disasters in Bangladesh’s garment industry.
On November 24, 2012, a fire at Tazreen Fashions in Nishchintapur, Ashulia, Dhaka, killed 114 workers and injured more than 200.
Marking the 14th anniversary of the tragedy, leaders and activists of various labour organisations held programs to remember those killed and demand rehabilitation for the injured.
More than a decade after the fire, many injured workers have yet to return to normal life. They say most promises of rehabilitation and proper medical treatment remain unfulfilled.
On Tuesday morning, activists of several labour organisations formed a human chain in front of the Tazreen Fashions factory in Nishchintapur, Ashulia. They also paid tribute to the victims by placing flowers at a makeshift memorial.
The fire broke out in a warehouse on the ground floor of the factory on the evening of November 24, 2012, and quickly spread throughout the nine-storey building. Many workers could not escape because the ground-floor exit was locked.
Some workers jumped from the upper floors to escape the flames. Many survived but sustained serious injuries, including fractures to their arms, legs, ribs and hips. Despite years of recovery, many have been unable to resume normal lives.
Official figures show that 114 workers were killed and more than 200 injured in the fire. Labour leaders, however, claim that more than 1,000 workers were injured, including 172 who were permanently disabled. Many are no longer able to work, leaving them struggling to earn a living while dealing with lasting physical injuries.
After the fire, various commitments were made to provide medical treatment, rehabilitation and employment for the injured workers. However, most of these promises have not been fulfilled, labour leaders alleged. Many continue to live in hardship without access to the medical care and rehabilitation they need.
At Tuesday's human chain, labour leaders demanded that the damaged factory building be demolished and replaced with housing for injured workers and a hospital for workers.
They also called for compensation equivalent to the lifetime earnings of each worker killed, proper medical treatment and employment opportunities for injured workers, and the prosecution of the factory owner and others responsible for the fire.
Fourteen years after the Tazreen fire, many injured workers are still struggling to rebuild their lives. Without rehabilitation and employment opportunities, they continue to wait for a chance to return to normal life.

Questions linger after Jensen Huang's return to Nvidia
item.description:
Jensen Huang's surprise return to Nvidia on Monday appeared to stabilize the US chip giant, along with the broader stock market and AI ecosystem, but questions linger about the long-term impact of his scandal.
An internal investigation overseen by independent directors is still underway at Nvidia regarding concerns that Huang might have been the target of an espionage campaign by China.
US government officials, including President Donald Trump, assured Nvidia's board that reinstating the company's cofounder "poses no national security risk."
In parallel, the US Department of Justice is investigating Megaspeed, a company based in Singapore that allegedly bought processors from Nvidia and routed them to Chinese customers, circumventing US export restrictions.
The Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) has also reportedly launched an investigation into Nvidia's accounting practices and potentially misleading communication to shareholders.
However, the Trump administration has generally avoided going after its allies, so the federal probes might not result in much, Columbia University Professor Eric Talley said.
The embattled chief will nevertheless have to explain himself to lawmakers at a closed-door hearing on December 1 before three House committees.
He will also testify before a Senate committee on December 3 in a hearing that will be livestreamed, while California's attorney general has opened an investigation into the company's chip exports and shareholder disclosures.
There are plenty of regulators who are willing to push back against the Trump administration and ask tough questions, Talley said.
Trump is also known to flip on people whom he no longer considers friends.
"He can become estranged with people, and if that would happen with Jensen Huang, I can imagine a boomerang" on the Trump administration's approach, Talley said.
Openly opposed to Huang's return before ultimately reinstating him, the board is in a delicate position. Former Goldman Sachs chief Lloyd Blankfein predicts its days may be numbered.
A revolt by shareholders, many of whom supported the reinstatement of the 63-year-old entrepreneur, could reshape the board as soon as 2027, since all directors stand for reappointment every year.
If they are spared, the directors could keep Huang on a much "shorter leash" compared to its history of largely deferring to the overwhelming power of this extraordinary executive, Talley said.
"The world is not the same as it was two weeks ago," AI researcher and commentator Gary Marcus wrote on X. "Nvidia is still down a third from what its peak was... (and) reporters are digging around much harder."
Since Huang's resignation, news articles have chipped away at the image of an upbeat, benevolent leader, instead portraying him as a difficult boss and revealing allegations of verbal abuse.
The board's decision "further amplifies the notion that big 'tech bros' don't need to play by the rules like the rest of us do," J. Gold Associates analyst Jack Gold said.
Observers expect a short-term rebound on Wall Street, driven by AI stocks, which began as early as Monday.
AI stocks have fueled the markets over the past two years, but there's still "a lot of noise about financing, geopolitics, durability and skepticism, even though companies across the AI supply chain keep reporting strong demand," Gabelli Funds portfolio manager Hendi Susanto said.
